name: Community robot arm - v6, simplified with base rotation
_notes: The linkage is planar and lives in a vertical half-plane that pivots about
the base axis. Inside that plane the coordinates are r (outward from the
axis, and may go negative when an arm folds back over the base) and z (up).
Plane angles: 0 degrees points along +r, 90 degrees points along +z.
So -90 is straight down, parallel with the base axis.
base.rotation is treated as just another control arm, named so it appears
alongside the others in robot.angles, in the step CSVs and in movements.
role 'control'  - you drive this angle
role 'fixed'    - the angle never changes (the tool arm)
angle_relative_to: leave it out for an angle measured from the plane itself
(what a parallelogram linkage gives you), or name another arm to measure
from that arm instead.

chain.name: main_arm
chain._note: driven through the parallel linkage from control_arm_b, so its angle is absolute in the r-z plane. Because base, elbow_a, joint and elbow_b form a parallelogram, this angle is exactly control_arm_b + 180 - which is where the limits come from: control_arm_b's -5 and (control_arm_a - 5), each shifted by 180.

chain.name: tool_arm
chain._note: horizontal, pointing away from the base axis: same z at both ends, and it swings round with the base so it always points outward. The arm reaches into negative r, so outward is 180 degrees in the plane, not 0.

_notes: How a joint angle from v6 becomes a servo angle for servo_control.py.
servo_angle = servo_at_zero + degrees_per_unit * joint_angle
degrees_per_unit is 1.0 for a servo coupled straight to the joint, -1.0
if it turns the other way, and the gear or pulley ratio if there is a
reduction in between.
servo_at_zero is what the servo reads when the joint is at 0 degrees -
which for most of these joints is outside their travel, so it is a
reference point rather than a pose you can stand the arm in.
The numbers below are placeholders that put each joint's whole range
inside the servo's safe travel. Calibrate them on the real arm before
running anything: servo_map.py has a solve_offset() for exactly that.
degrees_per_second is roughly how fast the servo slews unloaded, used
to work out how long to wait between steps. Measure it and lower it -
a loaded arm is slower, and waiting too little means the next setpoint
arrives before the servo has arrived.
